| **Mapping and software path** | Compiler-generated end-to-end execution using pinned mapping, compiler, runtime, driver and firmware versions where applicable, and interface versions. | No claim that the array is usable by the target stack. |
| **Interface and memory cost** | Offload granularity, bandwidth, traffic, latency, and a calibrated or validated energy-and-power model with execution rate, duty cycle, leakage and idle power, and the complete subsystem boundary. | No 3\ W or system-speedup claim. |
| **Cheap-screen validity** | Representative random or stratified target samples checked against a separate property-specific reference path, with class-specific error limits, uncertainty, the ability to decline a prediction when support is inadequate, and a later drift audit. | SCALE-Sim remains a source-study tool, not a target decision filter. |
| **RTL behavior** | Independently derived reference tests and properties where practical, plus lint, functional simulation, synthesis, and formal checks within their stated reach; add fault- and threat-model properties required by the target. | No implementation-readiness, reliability, or security claim beyond the properties checked. |
| **Physical behavior** | Pin the selected 3\ nm-class low-power process design kit, libraries, and process, voltage, and temperature conditions; then test area and floorplan feasibility, relevant setup and hold corners, congestion and design rules, routed dynamic and leakage power, power delivery, and electrothermal behavior. | No signoff, tapeout, or physical-feasibility claim. |
| **Containment** | Exercise each proposed bypass, disable, guardband, isolation mechanism, or fallback against the fault or attack it is intended to contain. | No claim that the implementation can contain or recover from that failure. |
| **Operational readiness** | Confirm required tool access; have qualified operators execute and challenge representative target cases within the allocated review capacity; record the named decision authority. | No claim that the transferred workflow can be operated, challenged, or used to support a target commitment. |

: **Each obligation changes what the next evaluation must measure.** Untested
boundaries remain visible rather than being absorbed into a general claim.
{#tbl-ch9-target-tests tbl-colwidths="[22,46,32]"}

Workload coverage and candidate comparison define the target architecture
question. Transfer benefit is separate and applies only when the study claims
that source structure helps relative to a target-only version. A claim that an
assisted workflow is advantageous also requires the matched complete-workflow
comparison owned by @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. The executable
path and interface costs then establish whether the candidate can run, while
cheap-screen, RTL, physical, containment, and operational-readiness checks
bound what the target result can support.

Three compact transfer cases show how the same reasoning applies beyond the
array study (@tbl-ch9-transfer-stress-tests). Each names the transfer unit, the
dependency that changed, a valid action, and the target check. The cases differ
deliberately. The first is an author-constructed transfer case. CircuitNet
provides congestion-prediction data and tasks
[@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet], while ChiPBench provides end-to-end physical
placement and PPA evaluation [@WangEtAl2025ChiPBench]. Neither source reports
the combined transfer procedure posed here. The other cases concern continuing
software improvement on fixed hardware and a physical defect that software
could not correct.

| **Transfer unit** | **Changed dependency** | **Valid action** | **Required target check** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Author-constructed transfer case for a learned congestion predictor trained on one process, library, and design family | The target process, library, netlist family, placement flow, or routed-result definition changes. | Requalify the unchanged predictor first; recalibrate, adapt, retrain, or retire it only after identifying what no longer holds. | Measure class-specific target error and decision quality against routed target results kept separate from calibration or training data. |
| H100 software-optimization result reported between MLPerf Training v2.1 preview and v3.0 [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware] | A later compiler, library, workload, or hardware generation changes the paired configuration. | Narrow the published improvement to its reported versions and workload; rerun the comparison for the new pair. | Repeat the end-to-end workload measurement with both hardware and software versions pinned and the same result definition. |
| Cougar Point containment and correction result [@Intel2011CougarPoint] | The target defect and the mechanisms able to reach it differ. Intel's announced permanent correction used revised silicon and repair or replacement; the release did not present firmware as the correction. | Do not assume a firmware-only remedy can reach a silicon defect; use a correction or containment mechanism matched to the failure. | Exercise the corrected silicon and any proposed containment against the target failure class before claiming correction. |

: **The same transfer test applies to learned, software, and physical
components.** The action follows the changed dependency, and the target check
must observe the failure or improvement being claimed.
{#tbl-ch9-transfer-stress-tests tbl-colwidths="[24,29,23,24]"}

The learned-predictor case prevents a familiar model name from substituting for
target support. The H100 case preserves the reported result without turning 17
percent into a general software-improvement rate. The Cougar Point case
preserves the lesson about failure reach without assuming that every silicon
defect requires the same remedy. All three retain useful source knowledge while
refusing to move the conclusion beyond the configuration that produced it.

Transfer does not change decision rights. Automated components may propose or
screen candidates inside the declared study.
Rejection, waivers, the architecture freeze, signoff, and tapeout remain with
the named roles defined in @sec-what-architect-owns.

The adaptation decision is complete even though the target architecture
decision is not. The study structure and reference candidate can move forward.
The source conclusion cannot.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Claiming transfer benefit against an unmatched target comparator.** If the
  target-only alternative receives different data, tools, tuning, or budgets,
  or the accounting omits adaptation, requalification, integration, checking,
  retirement, and recovery, harmful or cost-neutral reuse can appear beneficial.

- **Confusing drift with a new design problem.** Treating changed objectives,
  legal actions, or acceptance rules as ordinary drift can lead to recalibration
  against obsolete decision semantics, while treating every component change as
  a redesign needlessly repeats checks for unaffected claims.

## Open Questions

Transfer is not a property of a result in isolation. It depends on which data,
models, interfaces, tools, and conclusions retain their meaning after the
target changes.

**Scoping requalification.** The first problem is to limit requalification
without preserving stale claims or reusing the wrong design problem.

- **How can an AI-assisted architecture system identify the system-wide
  dependencies and claims needed for the smallest sound requalification set
  after a hardware or software version change?** Hidden dependencies can make a
  reduced set appear sufficient while leaving an invalid claim untouched. The
  selection succeeds only if it finds the affected claims that full cross-layer
  requalification would find while requiring less target checking.

- **How can an AI-assisted architecture system distinguish a target change
  that requires limited requalification from one that creates a new design
  problem?** A changed objective or legal choice can invalidate the source question even
  when many artifacts still match. The boundary should agree with independent
  architecture review on which prior claims remain relevant and which changes
  require a newly formulated study.

**Predicting useful transfer.** A design system must determine whether a
transferred component can improve the target decision enough to justify
requalification and integration work.

- **Which source-to-target invariants predict whether a learned architecture
  component is worth transferring?** Source accuracy cannot answer this
  question because preserved behavior can fail under changed target
  conditions. A useful invariant should predict target decision quality and
  requalification cost better than source accuracy or simple source-target
  similarity.

- **How can an AI-assisted system detect interaction failures where a
  transferred component meets a changed interface?** A component may retain its
  local behavior while the compiler-to-ISA mapping, RTL-to-memory contract,
  predictor-to-tool-version relation, timing assumption, or software interface
  changes around it. A useful detector should catch these target interaction
  failures with less checking than repeating every source check.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Transfer components, not conclusions"}
Reuse a data source, model, interface, tool path, or check only while its
invariant and dependencies still hold for the target. Recheck every claim
affected by a changed workload, software version, library, process condition,
interface, objective, or constraint, and recheck each unchanged component that
meets a changed neighbor. Carry the source record forward, but narrow or
withhold its conclusion until target evidence supports it.
:::

The five-step transfer method first compares the source and target decisions,
then separates the source into units and identifies the affected slice. It
assigns an action to each unit before asking a separate question about evidence.
Every affected unit receives a target check, and any claim that transfer itself
helps receives a target-only comparison. The result is neither blanket reuse
nor blanket repetition. It is a component-specific account of what remains
valid and what evidence the target still needs.

For the Lighthouse target study, the retained simulator outputs and candidate
identities remain historical results. The target keeps 32 by 32 as a historical
reference, refreshes the workload and software state, measures the executable
and physical path, and requalifies SCALE-Sim only for the target cases it can
screen within declared error limits. The local score, failed explanation,
AI-contribution comparison, and recorded recommendation do not transfer into
the RTL decision.

The next chapter receives this source-to-target map, the versioned
hardware-software state, and the target checks that remain
(@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). It asks a different question. Across
repeated and varied studies, does the configured system
improve the architecture result, the total cost of reaching it, or both?
